1.note: Printed וערבונות; A. Freimann, Ma'agal Tov ha-Shalem (Berlin–Jerusalem 1921–34), p. 122, reads ועברונות, ʿevronot: books on the rules of the Jewish calendar and intercalation. Two letters are transposed in the 1885 printing.

2.he: ליל ג' מס' ויחי ד' טבת
2.note: The parts of the date do not agree. 4 Tevet 5538 was the Sabbath of Vayigash (3 January 1778); the night of Tuesday in the week of Vayeḥi was the evening of Monday 5 January, which was 7 Tevet. ד (4) may be a misprint for ז (7). The next dates follow the weekday. A. Freimann, Ma'agal Tov ha-Shalem (Berlin–Jerusalem 1921–34), p. 123, dates the entry 7 Tevet ("טבת 7, ג' הלילה"), which fits the bracketed date: 7 Tevet 5538 began on the evening of Monday 5 January 1778. The 1885 ד' is a misprint.

3.note: Probably the Marquis de Thomé, known in Paris in these years for his interest in mysticism (later as a follower of Swedenborg); not certain.

4.note: דח"א = David Ḥayyim Ariani, the Ḥida's travelling companion from Italy to Turin; so the index of A. Freimann, Ma'agal Tov ha-Shalem (Berlin–Jerusalem 1921–34) ("ארייאני דוד חיים (דח"א)"), which lists this page. The sword was part of formal court dress for the visit to Versailles.

5.he: לוירסאלייאס או רואי די ויש וירסאליאר שיווא רושו
5.note: French words in Hebrew letters, read as an address: וירסאלייאס "Versailles" (with the Hebrew ל, "to"); או "au" (or "à"); רואי "rue"; די ויש וירסאליאר "de Vieux Versailles", the rue du Vieux-Versailles, an old street near the château; שיווא רושו perhaps "Cheval Rouge", a common inn sign (cheva[l] rou[ge], with ש for the French j-sound). The street is probable; the Cheval Rouge is a guess. A hotel of that name stands in Versailles today (rue André-Chénier, said to date from 1676), but an inn of that name on this street in 1778 is not confirmed. Reading suggested by the owner.

6.note: A. Freimann, Ma'agal Tov ha-Shalem (Berlin–Jerusalem 1921–34), p. 123, spells it קאג'אס: Spanish caja, "box, case". The object itself is described as of glass that looks like cloth.

7.note: Read as the Marquise de Croix (or de Croÿ); not identified.

8.note: Samuel Jacob Ḥayyim Falk (about 1708–1782), the "Baal Shem of London", a kabbalist and alchemist who had a following among Christian nobles. The Ḥida's hostile judgment of him follows.

9.note: Probably China, Italian Cina, written with ג for the ch-sound; in part 8 (paragraph 105) the Ḥida writes מהג'ינא for "from China". The book of "broad palm leaves" is probably a palm-leaf manuscript from South or South-East Asia.

10.note: The verb is printed in abbreviated form (הסי'); from the context, he either put on or kept on his hat, and then took it off on reading the Ḥida's name.
